# Magnetic compass (`magnetic_compass`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/navigation.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Navigation, transport & exploration (`navigation`)
- Deps: helped by dead_reckoning_log_line, map_projection_charts
- Core idea: A steel needle stroked with a lodestone (natural magnetite) and floated on straw or balanced on a pin turns to point roughly north–south, in any weather and out of sight of land. For a ship's compass glue the needle under a card marked with 32 points, pivot it on a brass pin in a bowl with a lubber's line fixed to the ship's axis, hang it in gimbals, and keep iron away from it; re-magnetise the needle on the lodestone when it weakens. It tells the heading, not the position: it must be combined with speed and time (dead reckoning).
- Pitfalls:
  - Thinking the needle points to true north everywhere; the difference (variation) is several degrees and changes from place to place
  - Storing iron tools, cannon or nails next to the binnacle
  - Crediting Flavio Gioia of Amalfi (a later myth) or claiming the compass 'gave' longitude
  - Thinking the Han Chinese lodestone 'south-pointing spoon' was a ship's instrument; its use and date are disputed, and the sea compass is Song
- History: china: 1044 – Wujing zongyao describes a magnetised iron 'fish'; 1088 Shen Kuo describes the needle and its deviation; c. 1117 Zhu Yu's Pingzhou ketan reports compasses on ships at Guangzhou (late 1090s); europe: c. 1190 – Alexander Neckam describes the needle at sea; 1269 Petrus Peregrinus describes a pivoted needle with scale; c. 1300 dry pivoted compass with card in the Mediterranean (independent invention or transmission is disputed); islamic: 1232 – al-Awfi describes a fish-shaped compass; c. 1282 Baylak al-Qibjaqi describes a floating needle used at sea
- Read:
  - Petrus Peregrinus, Epistola de magnete (1269)
  - Joseph Needham, Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 4 part 1: Physics (1962)
  - Amir D. Aczel, The Riddle of the Compass (2001)
